## The idea

Hold a low C beneath the notes of C major and the scale stops behaving like an
undifferentiated list. Some notes blend with the drone. Others seem to lean
toward a neighbour, even when you hold them still. The drone supplies a centre,
and that centre gives each note a job.

A note's position relative to the centre is its *scale degree*. Degree 1 is the
*tonic*, the pitch that most readily feels like home. Degree 7 is the leading
tone: it lies one semitone below the tonic and presses upward toward it. Degree
5, the dominant, can support a pause while still leaving the phrase open. These
roles are difficult to infer from isolated notes. A B by itself is a pitch; B
held against C can sound like a sentence waiting for its last word.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 72
use_synth :sine

define :play_phrase do |notes|
  notes.each do |pitch|
    play pitch, release: 0.38, amp: 0.8
    sleep 0.5
  end
end

c_major = scale(:c4, :major).to_a

in_thread do
  play :c3, sustain: 15.5, release: 0.5, amp: 0.45
end

[[6, 7], [3, 2], [4, 4], [1, 0]].each do |from, to|
  play c_major[from], release: 0.7
  sleep 1
  play c_major[to], release: 0.9
  sleep 2
end

stem = [:c4, :e4, :g4, :a4, :g4, :e4]
[:f4, :g4, :b4, :c5].each do |ending|
  play_phrase stem + [ending, ending]
  sleep 1
end
```

Listen first to the direction of each two-note pair. B to C makes the clearest
arrival because the semitone closes against the drone. F to E relaxes by a
similar small motion, though with less force. Repeated G can rest without fully
arriving. The four longer phrases hold their opening constant and change only
the ending, so the different kinds of closure can be attributed to the final
degree rather than to rhythm or contour elsewhere.

## Change one thing

1. Replace the C drone with `:a2` and leave the melody untouched. The same MIDI
   addresses now orbit A. Notice how C becomes a colour inside A minor instead
   of the most convincing point of rest.
2. Change the B ending to `:bb4`. B-flat stands a whole tone below C, so the
   tight upward pull is gone. Compare the two endings at the same tempo before
   assigning the difference to the accidental.
3. Raise the final G to `:g5`. It is still degree 5, but its new register changes
   its weight and brightness. Listen for whether height makes the boundary seem
   more exposed, even though the scale-degree function is unchanged.

## Why it works

Scale degree is an index interpreted against a tonic. Change the tonic and the
same MIDI number acquires another index and another tendency. The raw address
has not changed; its meaning within the current musical structure has. This is
much like reading an array offset only after you know which array is in scope.

No single mechanism produces the entire sense of stability. Short melodic
distance encourages motion to a neighbour, and the semitone from degree 7 to 8
is especially tight. The drone changes the acoustic relation of every scale
note to the bass. Long habits of hearing tonal music add another layer of
expectation. Holding the drone fixed does not separate all those causes, but it
does give them a stable reference against which their combined effect is easy
to compare.

The longer phrase is a controlled experiment. Synth, rhythm, register, and the
first six notes remain fixed; only the ending changes. That economy is useful
because a richly varied melody can hide the effect under several simultaneous
changes. Here, if one ending closes more firmly, the changed scale degree is the
best explanation available.

## Take it further

Create a hash that maps degrees 1 through 7 to your own tension rating from 0 to
5. Then play all seven degrees over one unchanged tonic drone in a shuffled
order. For each trial, leave two beats for a judgement, print the degree, and
play the resolution route you chose. Begin with `use_random_seed 42` so a second
run presents the same order. The ratings are observations rather than official
answers; the useful result is the pattern you can hear and reproduce.
